svg.title: Storage-mode and capacity-sizing decisions for Fabric BI serving
svg.desc: An original decision diagram for serving Power BI from a Fabric lakehouse. The first branch chooses a storage mode: Import copies and refreshes data on a schedule; DirectQuery forwards every visual to the source live; Direct Lake reads Delta columns straight from OneLake, pairing import-like speed with DirectQuery-like freshness and no copy — the recommended default here. A second branch then sizes the capacity for a Direct Lake model: whether the model's resident column footprint fits under the chosen SKU's memory bound, and whether broad free-license report viewing forces F64 or larger regardless of load. A closing panel lists the implementation guardrails: keep tables V-Ordered with ~1 GB files and low-cardinality partitions, prefer append/merge over overwrite, keep vacuum retention longer than the framing cadence, and confirm Block Public Internet Access is off before rollout.
svg.text: Storage-mode & capacity-sizing decisions for Fabric BI serving
Import vs DirectQuery vs Direct Lake · does the model fit the SKU memory bound · does report reach force F64+ · implementation guardrails
DECISION 1 — STORAGE MODE FOR A LAKEHOUSE-BACKED SEMANTIC MODEL

g.title: Storage-mode decision — Import, DirectQuery, and Direct Lake differ by whether data is copied and whether queries hit the source live.
Import — fast in-memory queries but stale between refreshes; the whole model must be memory-resident to answer queries.
g.text: Copies data into a compressed in-memory
cache; whole model loads before answering.
Fast, but stale between scheduled refreshes,
and every refresh recopies the dataset.
Default 1 GB cap; large format lifts it to SKU memory.

g.title: DirectQuery — always fresh because every visual issues a live source query, but each render pays a round trip and is typically slower.
g.text: Forwards every visual as a live query to
the source, so results are always current.
No copy, but a round trip per render —
Fits when data must be to-the-second live.

g.title: Direct Lake on OneLake — reads Delta columns straight from OneLake, pairing import-like speed with DirectQuery-like freshness and no copy or refresh job.
g.text: Reads Delta columns straight from OneLake —
no copy and no refresh job to orchestrate.
Never falls back; skips SQL-endpoint coupling.

g.aria-label: Composite model option for oversized fact tables
g.title: Composite option — Direct Lake on OneLake supports composite models, so a very large fact stays Direct Lake while dimensions use Import or DirectQuery.
g.text: keep the big fact in Direct

svg.text: DECISION 2 — SIZE THE CAPACITY FOR THE DIRECT LAKE MODEL

g.aria-label: Decision: does resident footprint fit the SKU memory bound
g.title: Memory-fit decision — the SKU sets the per-model memory bound; estimate resident column footprint (VertiPaq DMVs) against it.
Fits — hot columns stay resident and queries run at import-like latency; size for sustained load, letting smoothing absorb spikes.
g.text: Hot columns stay resident → import-like latency.
Size for average sustained load; bursting and
smoothing (5–64 min for interactive) absorb spikes.
Estimate footprint from VertiPaq storage DMVs.

g.aria-label: Footprint over the bound — cold reads
g.title: Over the bound — columns fall back to on-demand cold reads from OneLake at peak; step the SKU up, trim the model, or split workloads.
g.text: Footprint over the bound → on-demand cold reads
from OneLake at peak (degradation, not an error).
Remedies: step the F-SKU up (each step doubles
memory), trim/aggregate the model, or isolate
heavy workloads onto a separate capacity.

g.aria-label: Decision: does broad free-license viewing force F64+
g.title: Report-reach decision — F64+ lets free-license users view reports; below F64 every viewer needs a paid Pro/PPU seat.

g.aria-label: F64 licensing floor for broad consumption
g.title: F64 floor — broad viewer reach forces F64 or larger regardless of compute load, so licensing can set the SKU, not throughput.
g.text: F64 can be a licensing floor, not a load floor
Yes → F64+ so viewers on a free license consume via
a workspace viewer role. Broad BI reach forces F64+
even if the model would fit a smaller SKU on memory.
No / small audience → a smaller F-SKU with paid seats
may be cheaper; take the larger of the two SKU floors.

g.title: Guardrails — write-side layout, mutation pattern, vacuum window, OneSecurity check, and the Block Public Internet Access go/no-go.
g.text: • Write V-Ordered Delta with a ~1 GB Optimized Write target and low-cardinality partitions (<100–200 distinct) so column loads stay cheap.
• Prefer append/merge over Overwrite — Overwrite wipes commit history and forces a full cold-state reload on the next query.
• Keep vacuum retention longer than the framing cadence, or a vacuum can delete the Parquet files the framed model is pinned to and queries fail.
• Keep a single table under 10,000 Parquet files (framing fails past that). Confirm Block Public Internet Access is OFF and check OneSecurity before go-live.

svg.text: Fabric Atlas — original diagram, July 2026. Not a Microsoft asset; item icons vendored under Microsoft's Fabric icon terms.
